response:
Yes, a party may seek an urgent provisional remedy from a court despite the existence of a mediation agreement. Under Section 3A(2) of the **Commercial Mediation Centre of Sri Lanka (Amendment) Act, No. 37 of 2005**, the requirement to obtain a certificate of non-settlement before instituting court proceedings does not apply when a party seeks relief in respect of any provisional remedy under Part V of the Civil Procedure Code **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-4]**.

In such instances, the court is permitted to entertain and determine the action, but only to the extent that it relates to the granting of such provisional remedy **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-4]**.
reference: Yes, but only for the provisional remedy. Section 3A(1) generally prevents a court from entertaining proceedings concerning a commercial dispute covered by a mediation agreement unless they are accompanied by the Section 3F certificate of non-settlement. Section 3A(2) creates an exception for provisional remedies under Part V of the Civil Procedure Code; the court may entertain and determine the action only so far as it concerns that provisional relief.

It  appears  from  the  material  pleaded  by  the  Petitioner that  in  1997  the  then  President  as  Head  of  State  and  of Government acceded  to  the  Optional  Protocol  and  made  a Declaration as follows:

'The Government of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka pursuant to Article (1) of the Optional Protocol recognizes the competence of the Human Rights Committee to receive and consider communications from individuals subject to the jurisdiction of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, who claim to be victims of a violation of any of the rights set forth in the Covenant which result either from acts, omissions, developments or events occurring after the date on which the Protocol entered into force for the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka or from a decision relating to acts, omissions, developments or events after that date. The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka also proceeds on the understanding that the Committee shall not consider any communication from individuals  unless it has ascertained that the same matter is not being examined or has not been examined under another procedure of international investigation or settlement.'

There are three basic components of legal significance in this Declaration relevant to the matter at issue - viz:

- (i) A conferment of the rights set forth in the Covenant on an individual subject to jurisdiction of the Republic;
- (ii)  A conferment of a right on an individual within the jurisdiction of the Republic to address a communication to the Human Rights Committee in respect of any violation of a right in the Covenant that results from acts, omissions, developments or events in Sri Lanka;
- (iii) A recognition of the power of the Human Rights Committee to receive and consider such a communication of alleged violations of rights under the Covenant.

Components 1 and 2 amount to a conferment of Public Law rights. It is therefore a purported exercise of legislative power which comes within the realm of Parliament and the People at a Referendum as laid in Article 4(e) of the Constitution cited above.

I  wish  to  add  that  the  purported  accession  to  the Optional Protocol in 1997 is inconsistent with Article 2 of the Covenant which requires a State Party to 'take the necessary steps in accordance with its constitutional processes……..to adopt such laws or other measures as may be necessary to give effect to the rights recognized in the ………..Covenant.' I  cited  the  European  Communities Act 1972 of the U.K as an  instance  in  point  where  steps  were  taken  to  give  effect to  a  treaty  obligation  before  the  treaty  came  into  force.  No such steps were taken to give statutory effect to the rights in the Covenant. Without taking such measures, in 1997 the Optional Protocol was acceded to purporting to give a remedy through  the  Human  Rights  Committee  in  respect  of  the violation of rights that have not been enacted to the law of Sri Lanka. The maxim ubi Jus ibi remedium postulates a right being given in respect of which there is a remedy. No remedy is conceivable in law without a right.

It held that the 1997 accession and declaration under the Optional Protocol could not, without constitutionally valid legislative implementation, confer domestic judicial power on the UN Human Rights Committee or create an internal mechanism to revise a final Sri Lankan judgment. The Committee's views therefore supplied no domestic basis for revision, and the application was dismissed.

## Executive Summary

The Supreme Court of Sri Lanka exercises sole and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 126(1) of the Constitution to determine infringements of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action [LAW-1]. Judicial review is strictly confined to state action, excluding purely private wrongs [LAW-3]. While the Court protects absolute rights like those under Article 11, it maintains a clear distinction between justiciable public law matters and non-justiciable private disputes [LAW-3, LAW-11]. International human rights obligations are not self-executing and cannot override the Constitution [LAW-8].

## Findings

### Jurisdictional Boundaries and Fundamental Rights
Under Article 126(1) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court possesses sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine questions relating to the infringement or imminent infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action [LAW-1]. This jurisdiction is distinct from general administrative law challenges, as it is specifically triggered by the violation of rights recognized in Chapter III or IV of the Constitution [LAW-1]. The Court has clarified that "executive or administrative action" encompasses the exertion of state power by any organ, agency, or instrumentality of the State exercising governmental functions [LAW-3].

### Justiciability: Public vs. Private Disputes
- **Public Law Matters:** The Court exercises jurisdiction where the action involves the exercise of state power, such as university admissions, which are considered governmental functions [LAW-3]. Environmental decision-making is also subject to judicial review, as the Executive's role in managing natural resources is not absolute and remains subject to the Court's duty to protect fundamental rights under Article 126(1) of the Constitution [LAW-4].
- **Private Disputes:** The Court distinguishes between state action and private wrongs. Wrongful acts by individuals, unsupported by state authority, are considered private wrongs and do not attract the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 126 of the Constitution [LAW-3].

### Article 11: Freedom from Torture
Article 11 of the Constitution provides that no person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment [LAW-10]. 
- **Nature of the Right:** It is an absolute right, subject to no restrictions or derogations, even in times of war or emergency [LAW-10, LAW-11]. It applies to all persons, regardless of citizenship or criminal status [LAW-10, LAW-11].
- **Evidentiary Standard:** To establish a violation, the Court examines whether the treatment crosses the "threshold" of severity, intensity, and cruelty [LAW-12]. The Court must thoroughly examine facts, corroborative evidence, and the respondents' versions to determine if the acts constitute torture [LAW-12, LAW-14].

### International Obligations
Domestic application of international human rights obligations is limited. The Supreme Court has held that the Government cannot act in a manner contrary to the Constitution of Sri Lanka to satisfy international committee decisions, as international instruments are not self-executing in a way that overrides the Constitution [LAW-8].

## Conclusion

The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction is strictly defined by the Constitution. While it serves as the guardian of fundamental rights under Article 126(1) of the Constitution, it requires clear evidence of "executive or administrative action" to intervene [LAW-1, LAW-3]. Matters of private contract or those lacking a nexus to state power remain outside this scope. Furthermore, while the Court gives full effect to absolute rights like Article 11, it maintains the supremacy of the Constitution over international human rights mechanisms [LAW-8, LAW-11].

Ratnayake confines a dispute arising solely from a lawfully governed contract to ordinary contract law unless executive or administrative action independently engages Article 12. Visuvalingam v. Liyanage recognizes standing for readers and the protected recipient side of expression, but upholds restrictions that are lawfully imposed under Article 15(7) in an emergency and are within the competent authority's reasonable, honest judgment; the applications were dismissed without costs. Karunathilaka v. Dayananda Dissanayake treats the silent act of voting as protected expression under Article 14(1)(a). The Commissioner's acquiescence in suspending postal-ballot arrangements and failure to use the statutory power to fix a fresh Provincial Council poll date produced a grossly unjustified delay and was unlawful, arbitrary and for a collateral purpose. Presidential immunity did not convert official presidential action into unreviewable action or prevent appropriate proceedings through the Attorney-General.

Abeywickrema v. Pathirana treats public office as a statutory status: resignation is effective only upon acceptance by the proper appointing authority, ultra vires acts are reviewable, and estoppel cannot confer power a public authority lacks. Podinilame and Premachandra show that gubernatorial discretion is not unfettered. Removal of provincial commissioners requires legally relevant reasons, while a Governor choosing a Chief Minister must use a fair, rational process grounded in credible evidence. Certiorari and quo warranto may quash unlawful decisions; mandamus can compel a lawful fresh decision but not the appointment of a named person.

Weerawansha v. Attorney-General is an interim-order authority, not a final merits judgment. It declined to suspend the entire P-TOMS structure but stayed identified provisions concerning governmental functions, the regional fund and location, while indicating lawful alternatives. SC/FR/58/2018 treats irrational application of school-admission criteria as an Article 12(1) infringement and orders admission. SC/FR/97/2021 requires subjective and objectively reasonable suspicion for arrest, treats false official assertions and unsupported detention as arbitrary, and granted declarations and State compensation. SC/FR/233/2018 emphasizes that Article 11 is absolute but factual allegations must still be proved on a balance of probabilities with a high degree of certainty; the evidentiary failure led to dismissal without costs.

Bulankulama v. Ministry of Industrial Development applies Articles 12(1), 14(1)(g) and 14(1)(h), public-trust reasoning, sustainable-development principles and lawful environmental assessment to restrain the proposed Eppawala project until comprehensive study, publication and Central Environmental Authority approval. Singarasa confirms the dualist limit: executive accession to an international procedure cannot transfer domestic judicial power or authorize revision of a final judgment without constitutional legislative implementation. The memo must distinguish declaratory relief, compensation, writs, mandatory directions, costs and limited interim stays, and must not present Weerawansha as a final determination.

A  deed  generally  consists  of  the  following  parts:  (1)  the  premises or  recitals  (ii)  the h a b e n d u m clause  (iii)  the t e n e n d u m clause  (iv)  the r e d d e n d u m clause  (v)  the  conditions  and (vi)  the  covenants.

The h a b e n d u m clause  in  a  conveyance  indicates  the  property  or estate  that  is  to  be  taken  over  by  the  grantee.  As  a  general  rule, when the quantum of the interest conveyed is mentioned the h a b e n d u m may qualify,  enlarge,  lessen  or  explain  the  property or estate  granted.

The t e n e n d u m clause  in  English  law  indicated  the tenure  by which the  grantee was to hold the land of the grant or but which  now simply says  that  the  land  is  to  be  held  by  the  grantee  without  mentioning of  whom.

Most  deeds  now  have  both  clauses  coupled  and  as  such  the relevant  part  of  the  deed  says:  "To  have ( h a b e n d u m ) and  to  hold ( t e n e n d u m ) " .

The r e d d e n d u m clause refers  to  that  which is to be paid or rendered.

Conditions  are  stipulated  before  the  covenants.

## Executive Summary

This memorandum outlines the legal framework governing land disputes in Sri Lanka, emphasizing the strict requirements for notarial execution under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and the procedural rigors of partition actions. Key findings indicate that non-compliance with notarial requirements renders a transfer void [LAW-1], [LAW-4], and that registered *lis pendens* serves as a critical mechanism to prevent alienation during litigation [LAW-7], [LAW-8]. Prescription claims are subject to specific statutory periods, which may be suspended in cases of legal disability [LAW-12], [LAW-15].

## Findings

### 1. Validity of Land Transfers and Notarial Execution
Under Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, any sale or transfer of immovable property must be in writing and signed by the party making the transfer in the presence of a licensed notary and two or more witnesses [LAW-4]. A deed is generally comprised of specific clauses, including the *habendum* and *tenendum*, which define the interest conveyed [LAW-1]. Failure to adhere to these requirements, or the use of an unlicensed notary, renders the instrument legally ineffective [LAW-4]. The objective of this Ordinance is to prevent fraud by mandating notarially attested documentation as the exclusive evidence of transfer [LAW-5].

### 2. Priority and Lis Pendens
Under Section 12 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, a *lis pendens* must be registered to bind a purchaser [LAW-8]. Once a partition action is registered as a *lis pendens*, Section 66(1) of the Partition Act (as consolidated) prohibits any voluntary alienation, lease, or hypothecation of the land until the final determination of the action [LAW-7]. Any such transaction attempted in contravention of this section is void [LAW-7].

### 3. Prescription and Disabilities
Section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance allows for a claim of title based on ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted possession adverse to the claimant [LAW-12], [LAW-13]. However, Sections 13 and 14 of the Prescription Ordinance provide statutory protection by suspending the running of prescription during periods of legal disability, such as minority [LAW-15]. For mortgage bonds, Section 5 of the Prescription Ordinance prescribes a ten-year period for recovery, while Section 6 governs written promises or guarantees, setting a six-year period [LAW-11], [LAW-14].

### 4. Partition Actions and Statutory Sales
Partition actions require strict compliance with procedural rules, including the filing of a declaration by an attorney-at-law confirming the inspection of land registers [LAW-9]. Where property is mortgaged, the rights of the mortgagee are protected under the statutory framework [LAW-5]. In cases of State-alienated land or specific institutional lending, certificates of sale signed by authorized entities (e.g., the National Savings Bank) serve as conclusive proof of title transfer [LAW-5].

## Conclusion

The legal position regarding the disputed land is contingent upon the strict adherence to notarial formalities and the timely registration of interests. Any transfer lacking proper attestation is void [LAW-4]. Furthermore, the existence of a *lis pendens* effectively freezes the title, preventing further encumbrances [LAW-7]. Parties seeking to rely on prescription must prove ten years of adverse possession, while being mindful that statutory disabilities may toll the limitation period [LAW-12], [LAW-15]. Litigation strategy must prioritize the verification of the notary's license at the time of execution and the status of the land register entries.

The roadmap must begin with validity, not registration. Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requires the prescribed written, signed and notarial form for transactions affecting immovable property. Rohan de Soyza demonstrates that an unlicensed notary and lack of simultaneous presence render a purported transfer void and justify cancellation of registration. Registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance governs notice and priority among competing instruments but does not manufacture validity. Gnanasambandam establishes that, where the deed is valid, a transferee who accepts land subject to an intrinsic condition to retransfer cannot escape that condition merely by not signing the deed.

Prescription must be classified by the cause of action. Sections 3 and 4 address adverse possession and possessory restoration; Sections 5, 6 and 9 respectively govern mortgage or bond claims, written obligations, and loss or damage. Raja Nanayakkara excludes the first day and permits filing on the next working day when the last day is a public holiday. Jayasena applies the statutory disability protections in Sections 13 and 14 where mortgage rights devolve on minors. Hatton National Bank v. Sellers Sports distinguishes the ten-year mortgage-bond period from the six-year guarantee period, with the guarantee claim accruing when the stipulated written demand is not met.

Abeykoon v. National Savings Bank shows that a special statutory certificate-of-sale mechanism may pass title without an ordinary notarial conveyance, the specific enactment prevailing over general formal law. Recovery of Loans by Banks similarly requires attention to its notice, resolution, sale and certificate machinery. Land Development Ordinance permits and grants carry statutory conditions, restrictions on disposition, mortgage and execution, and special succession rules that ordinary private conveyancing cannot override.

Procedurally, the Civil Procedure Code requires material facts, cause of action, jurisdiction and relief to be properly pleaded; injunction applications under Sections 662-667 require petition and affidavit and expose the applicant to compensation if improperly obtained. A partition action must be registered as lis pendens, followed by statutory notice and survey, investigation of title, interlocutory decree and final partition or sale. Samuel Gnanam is relevant where partnership parties or Section 18 formal objections arise: initial capital and agency among partners must be proved rather than assumed. Fernando v. Mendis and Rawanna are not land authorities and should not be used to resolve title. The final advice must separately identify deed invalidity, priority, limitation, State-land restrictions, banking remedies and procedural preservation steps.

## Executive Summary
This memorandum outlines the regulatory requirements for a Sri Lankan company engaging in the sale of connected devices. Key compliance areas include the mandatory conversion of legacy bearer shares under the Companies (Amendment) Act, No. 12 of 2025 **[LAW-1]**, strict beneficial ownership disclosure obligations **[LAW-5]**, and the invalidity of exclusion clauses in consumer hire-purchase agreements under the Unfair Contract Terms Act, No. 26 of 1997 **[LAW-7]**. Furthermore, commercial disputes referred to mediation require a certificate of non-settlement before court proceedings can be initiated under the Commercial Mediation Centre of Sri Lanka (Amendment) Act, No. 37 of 2005 **[LAW-12]**.

## Findings

### Corporate Compliance: Bearer Shares and Beneficial Ownership
Under Section 51(1A) of the Companies Act, No. 07 of 2007 (as amended), companies are prohibited from issuing bearer shares **[LAW-4]**. Holders of existing bearer shares must convert them into registerable form within sixty days of the operation of the Companies (Amendment) Act, No. 12 of 2025; failure to do so results in the nullification of rights associated with those shares **[LAW-1]**. Additionally, companies must maintain a register of beneficial owners and appoint an authorized person residing in Sri Lanka to manage these records and facilitate disclosures to regulatory authorities upon request under Section 130C of the Companies Act, No. 07 of 2007 **[LAW-5]**.

### Consumer Protection and Hire-Purchase Agreements
Hire-purchase agreements are governed by the Consumer Credit Act, No. 29 of 1982 **[LAW-6]**. Owners must provide the cash price of goods in writing to the hirer before the agreement is entered into **[LAW-6]**. Under Section 7 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act, No. 26 of 1997, any contract term attempting to exclude or restrict liability for breaches of obligations arising from the Consumer Credit Act, No. 29 of 1982, is of no effect **[LAW-7, LAW-10]**. Furthermore, terms excluding liability for loss or damage resulting from defective goods in consumer use are void **[LAW-7, LAW-10]**.

### Commercial Mediation and Litigation
Where parties have agreed to refer disputes to mediation, Section 3A of the Commercial Mediation Centre of Sri Lanka (Amendment) Act, No. 37 of 2005, mandates that no court action may be instituted unless accompanied by a certificate of non-settlement issued under Section 3F **[LAW-12, LAW-13]**. 

| Process | Legal Requirement |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Settlement** | Must be in writing, signed, and is enforceable as a contract **[LAW-15]** |
| **Non-Settlement** | Mediator must issue a certificate to allow court access **[LAW-15]** |
| **Provisional Relief** | Court may grant provisional remedies under the Civil Procedure Code despite mediation requirements **[LAW-12]** |

For disputes under the Companies Act, No. 07 of 2007, parties may refer matters to the Companies Disputes Board. If a settlement is reached, a certified copy filed in court has the effect of a court judgment under Section 508(3) **[LAW-11, LAW-14]**.

## Conclusion
The company must prioritize the immediate conversion of bearer shares and the appointment of a local authorized person for beneficial ownership reporting. Standard form contracts must be reviewed to ensure they do not contain prohibited exclusion clauses regarding consumer hire-purchase obligations. Finally, the company should ensure that any mediation clauses in its contracts are aligned with the requirement to obtain a certificate of non-settlement before pursuing litigation.

*Note: Information regarding the specific validity of electronic signatures under the Electronic Transactions Act No. 19 of 2006 was not provided in the source documents and is therefore excluded.*

The company has corporate personality and broad capacity under Section 2 of the Companies Act, but contracts must be executed through Section 19-compliant authority and directors remain subject to Sections 187-190. The 2025 amendment requires legacy bearer instruments to be disclosed and converted within the statutory sixty-day period, with rights nullified on non-compliance, and introduces detailed beneficial-owner identification, company and Registrar registers, event-driven notifications and transitional reporting under Sections 130A-130J.

Electronic form alone cannot deny validity. The Electronic Transactions Act recognizes electronic records, signatures and contracts formed through automated message systems, subject to its attribution, dispatch, receipt and error rules and statutory exclusions. The Sale of Goods Ordinance then governs sale versus agreement to sell, description, quality and fitness, delivery, acceptance and remedies. Fernando v. Mendis treats a refusal to pay unless the seller accepts a new term as potential repudiation; Rawanna requires actual readiness and a request to take delivery before Section 37 non-acceptance loss may be recovered. Croos v. De Soysa limits 'goods' to tangible corporeal movables, so an assignment of an incorporeal monopoly right lies outside that regime.

Consumer-facing terms also engage the Consumer Affairs Authority Act. The Authority may inquire into timely written complaints about non-conforming goods and warranties, and implied consumer warranties and prohibitions on misleading conduct cannot simply be drafted away. Hire-purchase transactions require pre-contract cash-price disclosure, a signed agreement containing the prescribed price, instalment, deposit, goods and notice information, and delivery of a copy; enforcement and repossession rights are restricted by the Consumer Credit Act. The Unfair Contract Terms Act makes exclusions for death or personal injury from negligence ineffective and subjects other negligence exclusions and specified standard-form or consumer terms to reasonableness.

The Civil Law Ordinance imports English commercial law for specified subjects only where Sri Lankan written law does not otherwise provide. A contractual mediation clause triggers Sections 3A-3F of the Commercial Mediation Centre amendment: substantive proceedings ordinarily require a certificate of non-settlement, mediation communications are protected, a signed settlement is enforceable as a contract, and urgent provisional remedies remain available on a limited basis. The memo should end with an implementation checklist covering corporate registers, contracting authority, online assent records, consumer disclosures, hire-purchase documentation, delivery evidence, reasonable limitations and dispute-escalation language.

## Executive Summary

This memorandum addresses the legal framework for prosecuting and defending money laundering charges under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006. Key findings indicate that a conviction for the underlying predicate offence is not required for a money laundering conviction [LAW-11]. While confessions to police are generally inadmissible under the Evidence Ordinance, information leading to the discovery of property remains admissible [LAW-6, LAW-10]. Forfeiture of assets is mandatory upon conviction, subject to the protection of bona fide third-party interests [LAW-14].

## Findings

### Substantive Offence, Attempts, and Abetment
Under Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, the offence of money laundering is committed by any person who engages in transactions, receives, possesses, conceals, or disposes of property derived from unlawful activity, knowing or having reason to believe it is so derived [LAW-11]. Section 3(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, extends liability to any person who attempts, conspires, aids, or abets the commission of money laundering, with 'abet' defined by reference to Sections 100 and 101 of the Penal Code [LAW-11].

### Proof of Predicate Unlawful Activity
Section 3(3) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, explicitly declares that a conviction for the commission of the underlying unlawful activity is not necessary to prove the offence of money laundering [LAW-11].

### Admissibility of Confessions and Discovered Information
Under Section 25(1) of the Evidence Ordinance, a confession made to a police officer is inadmissible against an accused [LAW-7]. Furthermore, Section 26(1) of the Evidence Ordinance stipulates that a confession made while in police custody is inadmissible unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate [LAW-6, LAW-9]. However, under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance, if information received from an accused in police custody leads to the discovery of a fact (such as property), so much of that information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered is admissible, regardless of whether it amounts to a confession [LAW-6, LAW-10].

### Forfeiture and Bona Fide Third Parties
Upon conviction for money laundering, Section 13(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, mandates that the High Court order the forfeiture of property derived from unlawful activity to the State [LAW-14]. However, Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006, provides a safeguard, requiring the Court to consider whether such an order would prejudice the rights of a bona fide purchaser for value or any other person who has acquired a bona fide interest in the property [LAW-14].

### Statutory Presumption of Disproportionate Assets
The provided source documents do not contain specific provisions regarding a statutory presumption of guilt based solely on the possession of assets disproportionate to known income. The current framework focuses on the nexus between the property and the 'unlawful activity' as defined in the Act [LAW-11].

## Conclusion

The prosecution must establish that the accused dealt with property derived from unlawful activity with the requisite knowledge. While the prosecution is relieved of the burden of securing a conviction for the predicate offence [LAW-11], they must rely on admissible evidence—specifically information leading to the discovery of property under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance—to link the assets to the unlawful activity [LAW-6, LAW-10]. The defence should focus on challenging the nexus between the assets and the alleged unlawful activity and protecting the interests of any bona fide third parties under Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, No. 5 of 2006 [LAW-14].

Section 3 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act criminalizes specified transactions and dealings with property derived or realized from unlawful activity where the accused knew or had reason to believe its illicit origin. Attempt, conspiracy, aiding and abetting carry the same punishment, and the Act adopts the Penal Code meaning of abetment. A conviction for the predicate unlawful activity is not a prerequisite to proving laundering, but the prosecution must still establish the statutory elements and the link to unlawful activity. Section 4 creates a rebuttable presumption where money or other property cannot be reconciled with known income or receipts.

Admissibility must be separated from substantive proof. Evidence Ordinance Section 24 excludes a confession caused by a relevant inducement, threat or promise. Sections 25 and 26 prohibit proof of a confession to police or while in police custody unless the custodial confession is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. Section 27 permits only so much of the accused's information as distinctly relates to the fact discovered. Section 30 prevents a co-accused's confession from being considered against another jointly tried accused.

Criminal Procedure Code provisions governing police statements restrict their evidentiary use and do not permit routine corroboration by the prior police statement. Section 127 allows a Magistrate to record a confession only after inquiry supplies reason to believe it was voluntary and requires the prescribed memorandum. The prosecution must therefore prove voluntariness, compliance and independent evidence rather than treating the police narrative as substantive proof.

Upon conviction, Section 13 authorizes forfeiture of property derived from money laundering and addresses property disproportionate to known sources. Section 14 preserves a procedure for persons asserting bona fide interests. The memorandum should identify the prosecution's asset trail, source-of-funds and knowledge evidence; the defence challenges to the presumption and chain of custody; the limited Section 27 discovery evidence; and third-party ownership claims. It should not assume that an inadmissible confession becomes admissible merely because the alleged offence is serious.

## Executive Summary

This memorandum outlines the compliance obligations for a Sri Lankan employer, specifically addressing labour standards, dispute resolution, and trust-based asset management. Key findings include mandatory holiday and leave entitlements under the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act, the finality of Labour Tribunal orders under the Industrial Disputes Act, and strict identity-record keeping for express trusts under the Trusts (Amendment) Act. Please note that the provided sources do not contain specific minimum wage figures for 2025 or specific statutory requirements for marriage-capacity checks for employee benefits.

## Findings

### Employment Standards: Hours, Holidays, and Leave
Under Section 5 of the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act, every employee is entitled to one full holiday and one half-holiday per week, provided they have worked at least 28 hours in that week [LAW-4]. Regarding annual leave, Section 6 of the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act mandates specific annual holiday entitlements based on the commencement date of employment, with 14 days of full-remuneration leave granted for the second and subsequent years of service [LAW-5]. Additionally, employees are entitled to seven days of leave for private business, ill health, or other reasonable causes [LAW-5].

### Termination and Labour Tribunal Remedies
Under Section 31C of the Industrial Disputes Act, Labour Tribunals are empowered to conduct inquiries into employment terminations and issue orders that are "just and equitable" within six months of an application [LAW-6]. Applications must be filed within six months of the termination date [LAW-6]. Under Section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act, a tribunal may grant relief notwithstanding contrary terms in a service contract [LAW-9]. Once a matter is concluded before a Labour Tribunal, the employee is generally barred from seeking other legal remedies for the same issue [LAW-9].

### Public Servants (Liabilities) Ordinance
Under Section 2 of the Public Servants (Liabilities) Ordinance, no action can be maintained against a public servant for the repayment of money advanced or for debts/defaults, provided the public servant earns a salary of 520 rupees or less per month [LAW-7]. This protection does not apply if the public servant failed to disclose their status to the lender [LAW-7]. Employers should note that under Section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code, the wages of labourers and domestic servants, and portions of state officer salaries, are protected from execution of decrees [LAW-13].

### Trust-Held Assets and Identity Obligations
For family-owned enterprises utilizing express trusts, the Trusts (Amendment) Act imposes strict record-keeping duties. Under Section 19A, trustees must maintain and verify identity records for the author, trustees, beneficiaries, and agents every three months [LAW-15]. Failure to comply with these obligations, or failure to provide information to relevant authorities under Section 19B, constitutes an offence punishable by fines or imprisonment under Section 19C [LAW-14].

## Conclusion

Compliance requires strict adherence to the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act for leave and holiday management, and the Industrial Disputes Act for termination procedures. Employers lending to public servants must verify salary thresholds and disclosure status under the Public Servants (Liabilities) Ordinance. Finally, trustees must ensure rigorous identity verification for all parties involved in express trusts to avoid criminal liability under the Trusts (Amendment) Act. Information regarding 2025 minimum wage adjustments and marriage-capacity checks for benefits is not available in the provided documentation.

The Shop and Office Employees Act limits ordinary work to eight hours a day and forty-five hours a week and provides weekly, annual, casual and public-holiday entitlements with remuneration, subject to its detailed conditions and exceptions. The National Minimum Wage amendment sets Rs. 27,000 monthly and Rs. 1,080 daily for 1 April-31 December 2025, rising to Rs. 30,000 and Rs. 1,200 from 1 January 2026; specified budgetary relief allowances form part of those wages rather than an additional duplicate payment.

The Maternity Benefits Ordinance supplies paid maternity benefit and protected absence according to the statutory circumstances, prohibits termination merely because of pregnancy, confinement or consequent illness, places the burden on the employer to prove another reason, and restricts injurious work around confinement. Applicable coverage must be checked because shop and office employees may fall under the separate maternity provisions in the Shop and Office Employees Act.

The Service Contracts Ordinance deems most verbal servant contracts month-to-month with one month's notice, regulates wages on discharge, and imposes special form, explanation, certification, triplicate and duration requirements for covered written engagements exceeding one month. These historic provisions must be reconciled with later employment legislation. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, disputes may proceed through conciliation or arbitration; collective agreements and awards bind as provided; and a workman may apply to a labour tribunal concerning termination or gratuity, generally within six months, with reinstatement or compensation among the possible remedies.

The Public Servants (Liabilities) Ordinance can bar specified actions on loans, guarantees and securities against protected public servants, subject to the salary threshold and exceptions including non-disclosure of public-servant status. The Marriage Registration Ordinance generally requires both parties to have completed eighteen years and identifies prohibited relationships and subsisting-marriage restrictions; benefit administration should verify legal status without purporting to adjudicate it.

For an express trust, the Trusts amendment requires registration-related information, quarterly verification and updating of prescribed identity information, six-year post-involvement retention, identification of natural beneficial owners and disclosure to authorized anti-money-laundering bodies. The memo should end with separate payroll, leave, termination, lending, dependent-benefit and trust-record checklists rather than treating these enactments as a single employment code.

# Employment Agreement

## 1. TITLE AND PARTIES
This Employment Agreement is entered into on this `[DATE]` day of `[MONTH]`, `[YEAR]` by and between:

**Employer:** `[EMPLOYER NAME]`, having its principal place of business at `[ADDRESS]` (hereinafter referred to as the "Employer"); and

**Employee:** `[EMPLOYEE NAME]`, residing at `[ADDRESS]` (hereinafter referred to as the "Employee").

## 2. RECITALS / PREAMBLE
WHEREAS, the Employer operates a shop/office in Sri Lanka and requires the services of the Employee; and
WHEREAS, the Employee agrees to perform the duties of `[JOB TITLE]` under the terms and conditions set forth herein, in compliance with the laws of Sri Lanka.

## 3. DEFINITIONS
- **"Act"** refers to the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act, No. 19 of 1954 (as amended).
- **"Minimum Wage"** refers to the national minimum wage as prescribed by the National Minimum Wage of Workers (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2025 **[LAW-3]**.
- **"Year of Employment"** means the period of twelve months reckoned from the first day of January of each year **[LAW-6]**.

## 4. OPERATIVE CLAUSES
- **Remuneration:** The Employer shall pay the Employee a monthly wage of not less than thirty thousand rupees (LKR 30,000) effective from January 1, 2026, in accordance with **[LAW-3]**.
- **Working Hours and Intervals:** The Employee shall be allowed intervals for rest or a meal as required by the Schedule to the Act, including one hour between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. if the work period includes those hours **[LAW-2]**.
- **Annual Holidays:** The Employee is entitled to 14 days of annual holiday with full remuneration for each year of continuous employment, to be taken in the year succeeding the year of employment **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-4]**.
- **Casual Leave:** The Employee is entitled to 7 days of leave with full remuneration for private business or ill health, subject to the conditions of the Act **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-8]**.
- **Public Holidays:** The Employee shall be allowed holidays on public holidays as declared by the Minister, not exceeding nine days per year **[LAW-6]**, **[LAW-9]**.

## 5. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES
- The Employer warrants that this agreement does not modify or reduce any rights conferred upon the Employee by the Act to their detriment, and any such modification shall be null and void **[LAW-2]**.
- The Employee warrants that they are legally eligible to work in Sri Lanka.

## 6. TERMINATION
- Upon termination, the Employee is entitled to take accrued annual holidays for the preceding year and a pro-rata holiday entitlement for the current year of service as per **[LAW-8]**.
- Either party may terminate this agreement by providing `[NOTICE PERIOD]` written notice.

## 7. DISPUTE RESOLUTION
- This agreement shall be governed by the laws of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.
- Any disputes arising out of this agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the relevant Labour Tribunal or Court of competent jurisdiction in Sri Lanka **[LAW-7]**, **[LAW-10]**.

## 8. GENERAL PROVISIONS
- **Entire Agreement:** This document constitutes the entire agreement between the parties.
- **Severability:** If any provision is held to be invalid, the remaining provisions shall continue in full force and effect.

## 9. EXECUTION

**Employer Signature:** ____________________ Date: __________

**Employee Signature:** ____________________ Date: __________

**Witness 1:** ____________________

**Witness 2:** ____________________

## Notes for Completion
- `[PARTY A NAME]`, `[ADDRESS]`, `[DATE]`, `[MONTH]`, `[YEAR]`, `[EMPLOYEE NAME]`, `[JOB TITLE]`, and `[NOTICE PERIOD]` must be filled by the user.
- Ensure that any specific company policies regarding leave application procedures are attached as an addendum, provided they do not conflict with the statutory minimums cited in **[LAW-1]** and **[LAW-8]**.

The document must include recordkeeping, grievance, governing-law and notes-for-completion sections.

# Hire-Purchase Agreement

This Hire-Purchase Agreement (the "Agreement") is entered into on this `[DATE]` by and between:

**OWNER:** `[COMPANY NAME]`, a company incorporated in Sri Lanka with registered office at `[ADDRESS]` (hereinafter referred to as the "Owner"); and

**HIRER:** `[HIRER NAME]`, residing at `[ADDRESS]` (hereinafter referred to as the "Hirer").

## 1. Recitals
WHEREAS, the Owner is engaged in the business of selling household appliances;
WHEREAS, the Hirer desires to acquire the appliance described in the Order Summary (the "Goods") via a hire-purchase arrangement pursuant to the Consumer Credit Act, No. 29 of 1982 **[LAW-1]**.

## 2. Definitions
- **"Cash Price"**: The price at which the Goods may be purchased for cash, as disclosed in the Order Summary **[LAW-1]**.
- **"Hire-Purchase Price"**: The total sum payable by the Hirer to complete the acquisition of the Goods, including deposits and installments, excluding penalties **[LAW-5]**.
- **"Hirer"**: The person obtaining possession of the Goods under this Agreement **[LAW-5]**.

## 3. Operative Clauses
3.1. **Disclosure**: The Owner confirms that the Cash Price has been disclosed to the Hirer in writing prior to this Agreement **[LAW-1]**.
3.2. **Payment**: The Hirer shall pay the Hire-Purchase Price in installments as specified in the Order Summary. The Owner shall, upon written request and payment of one rupee, provide a statement of account showing amounts paid and future installments due **[LAW-6]**.
3.3. **Title**: The Owner’s title to the Goods shall vest in the Hirer only upon full payment of the Hire-Purchase Price ****.

## 4. Representations and Warranties
4.1. The Hirer warrants that all information provided for the electronic order process is accurate.
4.2. The Owner warrants that the Goods are of merchantable quality and fit for the purpose for which they are supplied, subject to statutory rights under Sri Lankan law.

## 5. Termination
5.1. The Hirer may terminate this Agreement in accordance with rights conferred by the Consumer Credit Act **[LAW-7]**.
5.2. Any provision in this Agreement attempting to exclude or restrict the Hirer’s statutory right to terminate is void **[LAW-7]**.

## 6. Dispute Resolution
6.1. **Mediation**: Any dispute arising out of this Agreement shall be referred to mediation in accordance with the Commercial Mediation Centre of Sri Lanka Act, No. 44 of 2000 **[LAW-3]**.
6.2. **Court Action**: No court action shall be instituted unless accompanied by a certificate of non-settlement, provided that this shall not apply to applications for provisional remedies under the Civil Procedure Code **[LAW-3]**.
6.3. **Governing Law**: This Agreement is governed by the laws of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.

## 7. General Provisions
7.1. **Notices**: Notices may be served by personal delivery, registered post, or ordinary post with a certificate of posting to the last known address **[LAW-8]**.
7.2. **Severability**: If any provision is found to be void under the Consumer Credit Act, such provision shall be severed without affecting the remainder of the Agreement **[LAW-7]**.

## 8. Execution
This Agreement may be executed via electronic signature, which shall be deemed valid and binding.

**Owner Signature:** ____________________
**Hirer Signature:** ____________________

## Notes for Completion
- `[DATE]`: Insert date of execution.
- `[COMPANY NAME]`, `[ADDRESS]`: Insert Owner details.
- `[HIRER NAME]`, `[ADDRESS]`: Insert Hirer details.
- **Order Summary**: Ensure a separate document or digital interface clearly lists the Cash Price, Hire-Purchase Price, and installment schedule as required by **[LAW-1]** and **[LAW-6]**.

The draft must end with client-input notes and should not invent prices or dates.

All dates, deed numbers, registry references, shares and survey details must remain placeholders.

response:
## Issue

Whether the deduction of marks for a school that does not function as a valid alternative government primary school, thereby preventing a child's admission to Grade 1 under the 'Residents in close proximity' category, constitutes an infringement of the Fundamental Right to equality guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and what relief is appropriate.

## Rule

1. **Article 12(1) of the Constitution**: Guarantees the right to equality and equal protection of the law, ensuring that among equals, the law should be applied equally **[LAW-5]**.
2. **Circular No. 22 of 2017 (Clause 6(III))**: Provides that marks are deducted at a rate of 5 marks for each "other government primary school" that is closer to the applicant's residence than the school applied for, provided the child can gain admission to such a school **[LAW-7]**.
3. **Criteria for Alternative Schools**: A school qualifies as an alternative only if it has a primary section where the child can gain admission **[LAW-6]**, ****.

## Application

Under Clause 6(III) of Circular No. 22 of 2017, the deduction of 5 marks is contingent upon the existence of an alternative government primary school where the child can actually gain admission **[LAW-7]**. If a school is identified as an alternative but lacks the capacity or status to admit the child (e.g., it does not function as a primary school or cannot admit the child), the deduction of marks is legally unjustified under the circular's own criteria **[LAW-5]**.

In the present scenario, the authorities incorrectly counted a school that does not facilitate Grade 1 intake as an alternative. By applying this deduction, the authorities effectively penalized the applicant based on an erroneous interpretation of the school's status. As established in *SC FR 58/2018*, when such an error results in a candidate falling below the cut-off mark—despite being otherwise eligible—it constitutes a failure to apply the law equally to those who meet the criteria. Consequently, the exclusion of the child from admission due to these improperly deducted marks infringes upon the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution **[LAW-5]**.

## Conclusion

The infringement of Article 12(1) is established when authorities misapply the criteria for mark deduction, thereby denying admission to an eligible candidate. The appropriate relief, as supported by the precedent in *SC FR 58/2018*, is for the court to direct the relevant authorities to restore the improperly deducted marks and grant admission to the child to the applied-for school (Grade 1 or the appropriate grade). This conclusion is highly certain based on the provided case law regarding the misapplication of Circular No. 22 of 2017 **[LAW-5]**.
reference:
Issue: Whether applying the admissions circular on a factually inapplicable premise amounts to unequal or arbitrary administrative treatment.

Rule: Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law. SC/FR/58/2018 held that a school that could not in fact admit the child as a government primary school should not be counted to reduce proximity marks. Once the wrongly deducted marks were restored, the child crossed the admission threshold and the respondents' refusal infringed Article 12(1). Roberts v. Ratnayake is distinguishable: that case concerned rights arising solely from a lawfully terminated contract, whereas school admission is an administrative decision governed by a public circular.

Application: A school with no Grade 1 intake is not a genuine alternative for the relevant admission. Deducting marks on that basis applies the circular irrationally. If the additional five marks place the child above the cut-off, the error is material and produces unequal administrative treatment.

Conclusion: The court should declare an Article 12(1) infringement and direct the principal or competent authority to admit the child to Grade 1 or, if time has passed, to the appropriate current grade.

## Issue

Whether the Governor's removal of members of the Provincial Public Service Commission (PPSC) for the purpose of 'reconstitution' and the subsequent appointment of new members is legally valid under the Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987, and what public-law remedies are available to challenge these actions.

## Rule

1. **Tenure and Removal**: Under Section 33(3) of the Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987, members of the PPSC hold office for five years unless they resign or are removed by the Governor "for cause assigned." 
2. **Requirement of Cause**: The Governor must provide specific reasons for removal to allow the affected members to make representations. Removal cannot be arbitrary, unreasonable, or based on unfettered discretion **[LAW-3]**, **[LAW-12]**.
3. **Appointment Power**: Under Section 33(1) of the Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987, the Governor has the power to appoint members to the PPSC **[LAW-11]**.
4. **Judicial Review**: Public law dictates that there is no "absolute or unfettered discretion." Courts may review appointments and removals for unreasonableness, bad faith, or reliance on irrelevant considerations **[LAW-12]**.

## Application

In the present scenario, the Governor removed the members of the PPSC solely to "reconstitute" the Commission. According to Section 33(3) of the Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987, removal must be "for cause assigned" **[LAW-3]**. The courts have established that "reconstitution" is not a valid cause for removal, as the Governor cannot remove members simply because he is "so minded" **[LAW-12]**. 

Furthermore, the Governor's failure to produce evidence of misconduct or incapacity renders the removal arbitrary and *ultra vires* **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-8]**. Because the removal of the original members was illegal, the subsequent appointments of the new members are consequential upon an illegal act and are therefore invalid **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-8]**. The Governor’s discretion is limited by the requirement that it be exercised reasonably and for the public good, rather than for political convenience or arbitrary restructuring **[LAW-12]**.

## Conclusion

The Governor's actions are legally invalid. The removal of the PPSC members without "cause assigned" violates Section 33(3) of the Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987. Consequently, the appointments of the new members are also void. 

Appropriate public-law remedies include:
1. **Writ of Certiorari**: To quash the Governor's orders removing the original members and the subsequent appointments of the new members **[LAW-4]**, ****.
2. **Writ of Quo Warranto**: To challenge the legal authority of the newly appointed members to hold their offices **[LAW-4]**, ****.

This conclusion is reached with high certainty based on the precedent that public functionaries cannot exercise unfettered discretion to remove statutory appointees without valid, assigned cause **[LAW-12]**.

Issue: Whether the Governor's statutory discretion permits removal without a legally sufficient reason and whether the replacement appointments survive the invalid removals.

Rule: Podinilame v. Mathew holds that public-law discretion is held in trust for the statutory purpose and is never absolute or unfettered. A bare desire to reconstitute the Commission is no cause; removal requires reasons sufficiently serious to bear on the members' ability to discharge their duties. Premachandra v. Jayawickrema further establishes that even where the Constitution entrusts an opinion to a Governor, the decision-making process remains reviewable for legality, rationality, relevant evidence and fairness. Undisclosed or unsupported assertions cannot outweigh firm, verifiable material.

Application: The stated reason does not address misconduct, incapacity or any statutory purpose. The immediate partisan replacements and refusal to disclose material support an inference of improper purpose, arbitrariness and a flawed process. The removals are ultra vires. Appointments made only because of those removals are consequentially unlawful.

Conclusion: Certiorari should quash the removal and appointment decisions, and quo warranto may challenge the new members' authority to hold office. If a fresh exercise of power is necessary, mandamus may require the Governor to act according to law, but should not dictate the identity of a particular appointee.

## Issue

Whether a transferor can enforce a condition for the retransfer of land contained in a notarial deed when the transferee did not sign the deed, and whether the validity of the deed is affected by the lack of a valid notary licence and the failure of parties/witnesses to sign in each other's presence.

## Rule

1. Under Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840, any sale, transfer, or agreement affecting immovable property must be in writing, signed by two witnesses in the presence of a Notary, and duly attested by said Notary to be of force or avail in law **[LAW-7]**.
2. A condition for retransfer intrinsic to a transfer deed binds the vendee even if the vendee has not signed the deed, as acceptance of the deed carries an implied assent to the conditions therein **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-10]**.
3. Courts will not allow a party to use the provisions of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance to effectuate a fraud or to take advantage of their own fraud **[LAW-10]**.

## Application

Regarding the enforceability of the retransfer condition, the law establishes that a vendee is bound by a condition subsequent attached to the property, even without their signature, because the obligation is intrinsic to the transfer itself **[LAW-1]**. The vendee's acceptance of the deed constitutes an implied assent to the conditions stipulated therein **[LAW-10]**.

However, the provided sources do not contain information regarding the specific legal consequences of a notary lacking a valid annual licence or the failure of parties and witnesses to sign in each other's presence. While Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840, mandates strict compliance with attestation requirements for a deed to be of "force or avail in law" **[LAW-7]**, the provided sources do not explicitly address whether a deed failing these specific procedural requirements remains enforceable or if it renders the entire instrument void.

## Conclusion

While the transferee's failure to sign the deed does not prevent the enforcement of a retransfer condition **[LAW-1]**, the enforceability of the deed itself is contingent upon the requirements of Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840 **[LAW-7]**. The provided sources do not contain sufficient information to determine the legal effect of an invalid notary licence or the failure of parties to sign in the presence of witnesses. Consequently, it is uncertain whether the transferor can enforce the condition if the deed fails to meet the statutory attestation requirements.

Issue: The scenario raises two distinct questions: whether a transferee who did not sign may avoid an intrinsic condition, and whether the deed was validly executed at all.

Rule: Gnanasambandam v. Bin Adaham holds that, where a valid deed transfers property subject to a condition subsequent, the transferee who accepts the encumbered title cannot detach the condition from the transfer merely because the transferee did not sign; acceptance of the benefit carries the intrinsic obligation to retransfer. Rohan de Soyza v. Jinendradasa holds, however, that a purported transfer executed before a notary without a valid annual licence and without the required simultaneous presence violates Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and is void; registration does not cure that foundational defect.

Application: If execution were otherwise valid, the transferee's non-signature alone would not defeat the retransfer condition. Here, the independent notarial and presence defects go to the legal existence of the transfer itself. A party cannot selectively enforce a condition in a deed that is void for failure to meet Section 2, although restitutionary or other relief may arise on separately pleaded facts.

Conclusion: The condition is not defeated simply by the transferee's non-signature, but it cannot be enforced as a term of this deed if the lack of a licensed notary and simultaneous execution is proved. The deed and its registration are vulnerable to cancellation.

## Issue

1. Whether the arrest of the activist violated Article 13(1) of the Constitution regarding the procedure established by law and the requirement of reasonable suspicion.
2. Whether the detention and the conduct of the authorities violated Article 11 (freedom from torture/cruel treatment) and other fundamental rights, given the lack of evidence for the assault claim.

## Rule

- **Article 13(1) of the Constitution**: "No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest." **[LAW-5]**
- **Reasonable Suspicion Standard**: Under the Prevention of Terrorism (Special Provisions) Act (PTA), an arrest requires that the arresting officer must subjectively form a suspicion, and there must objectively be a reason for such belief. **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-9]**
- **Burden of Proof**: The burden is on the respondent to prove that they subjectively formed the required suspicion and that there was objective material to support it at the time of the arrest. **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-9]**
- **Malice**: The inclusion of false assertions in a B-report (such as falsely claiming the Attorney-General advised an arrest) demonstrates malice and a failure to follow the procedure established by law. **[LAW-3]**

## Application

1. **Article 13(1) Violation**: The arrest was predicated on a press conference that, when read in its entirety, promoted ethnic harmony rather than disharmony **[LAW-9]**. Because the respondents failed to provide sufficient objective material to form a "reasonable suspicion" of unlawful activity, the arrest failed the objective test established in *Weerawansa v. Attorney General* **[LAW-1]**, **[LAW-9]**. Furthermore, the CID’s inclusion of a false assertion in the B-report regarding the Attorney-General’s advice constitutes malice and confirms that the procedure established by law was not followed **[LAW-3]**.

2. **Article 11 Claim**: While the activist alleges assault, the provided sources do not contain information regarding the substantiation of this claim. Under the provided rules, I must state that information regarding medical or corroborating evidence for the Article 11 claim is missing from the source documents. Consequently, a legal determination on the Article 11 violation cannot be made based solely on the provided text.

3. **Articles 12(1) and 13(2)**: The provided sources focus primarily on the procedural requirements of the PTA and Article 13(1). The sources do not provide specific facts or legal analysis regarding the application of Article 12(1) (equality before the law) or Article 13(2) (detention before a judge) to this specific activist's case.

## Conclusion

Based on the provided sources, the arrest of the activist violated Article 13(1) of the Constitution because the respondents failed to establish an objective basis for "reasonable suspicion" and acted with malice by including false information in the B-report **[LAW-3]**, **[LAW-9]**. The claims regarding Article 11, Article 12(1), and Article 13(2) cannot be analyzed due to a lack of sufficient information in the provided source documents. This conclusion is highly certain regarding the Article 13(1) violation based on the precedent of *sc_fr_97_2021*.
reference:
Issue: Whether the arrest and detention followed lawful procedure and whether the separate allegation of ill-treatment is proved to the required standard.

Rule: SC/FR/97/2021 requires both a genuinely held suspicion and objectively sufficient material for an arrest of this kind. Reading a speech as a whole matters; isolated words stripped of context cannot create reasonable suspicion. A false B-report assertion may evidence malice. Failure to establish the material supporting a detention order also undermines Article 13(2). Arbitrary illegality engages Article 12(1). For Article 11, SC/FR/233/2018 confirms that the right is absolute but the alleged acts must be proved on a balance of probabilities with a high degree of certainty; material gaps in medical and corroborative evidence may be fatal.

Application: The harmonious content of the speech, absence of objective material, non-production of the investigative basis and false statement support violations of Articles 13(1), 13(2) and 12(1). The assault allegation is analytically separate. Without medical records, consistent contemporaneous complaints, video support or other corroboration, a court may decline to find the high-probability factual basis required for Article 11.

Conclusion: The activist should succeed on arbitrary arrest, detention and equality claims, with a declaration and just and equitable compensation, but the Article 11 claim is likely to fail on proof rather than because the right is qualified.

## Issue

1. Whether the buyer’s refusal to pay for an instalment unless the seller provides an additional guarantee constitutes a repudiation of the contract, justifying the seller's refusal to make further deliveries.
2. Whether the seller is entitled to claim damages for storage losses regarding a shipment that was not placed at the agreed delivery point or offered to the buyer.

## Rule

1. Under Section 31(2) of the Sale of Goods Ordinance, in an instalment contract, whether a breach constitutes a repudiation of the whole contract or a severable breach depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances of the case.
2. As established in *Fernando et al. v. Mendis* (151-NLR-NLR-V-23), a refusal to pay that is conditional upon terms not found in the original contract constitutes a refusal to be bound by the contract, justifying the seller's refusal to make further deliveries.
3. Under Section 49(1) and (2) of the Sale of Goods Ordinance, a seller may maintain an action for damages for non-acceptance where the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay for goods, with damages measured by the loss directly and naturally resulting from the breach.

## Application

1. **Buyer's Counterclaim**: The buyer’s refusal to pay for the first shipment unless the seller provides a guarantee not stipulated in the contract mirrors the facts in *Fernando et al. v. Mendis* [LAW-3], [LAW-6]. In that case, the court held that such a conditional refusal is not a mere failure to pay, but a "definite refusal to pay, except upon terms" which are not within the contract [LAW-6]. Consequently, this conduct demonstrates an intention to repudiate the contract, justifying the seller's decision to cease further deliveries [LAW-6]. Therefore, the buyer's counterclaim for non-delivery is likely to fail as the seller was legally justified in treating the contract as repudiated.

2. **Seller's Claim for Storage Losses**: Under Section 49(2) of the Sale of Goods Ordinance, damages are limited to the loss "directly and naturally resulting" from the buyer's breach [LAW-7], [LAW-10]. If the seller failed to place the goods at the agreed delivery point or failed to offer them to the buyer, the seller has not fulfilled the requirements for performance under the contract [LAW-1], [LAW-9]. Without a valid tender of delivery, the buyer cannot be held in default for non-acceptance of those specific goods. Consequently, the seller cannot claim storage losses for goods that were never properly tendered or made available for delivery as per the contract terms.

## Conclusion

It is highly probable that the buyer's counterclaim for non-delivery will be dismissed, as their conditional refusal to pay constitutes a repudiation of the contract under Section 31(2) of the Sale of Goods Ordinance and the precedent in *Fernando et al. v. Mendis* [LAW-6]. Conversely, the seller's claim for storage losses is likely to fail because the seller failed to perform the necessary steps to tender delivery, thereby failing to establish the buyer's liability for those specific goods under Section 49 of the Sale of Goods Ordinance. This conclusion is based on the provided case law and statutory provisions; however, the outcome remains subject to the specific terms of the contract regarding delivery obligations.
reference:
Issue 1: Whether the buyer's qualified refusal to pay amounted to repudiation. Fernando v. Mendis distinguishes a mere delayed payment from a definite refusal to perform except on a new, extra-contractual term. The latter demonstrates an intention not to be bound and may justify withholding future deliveries. On these facts, the buyer's insistence on a new guarantee supports the seller's repudiation defence to the buyer's non-delivery claim.

Issue 2: Whether the seller may recover loss for non-acceptance of the later shipment. Section 37 of the Sale of Goods Ordinance, as applied in Rawanna & Co. v. Arunachapillai, requires proof that the seller was ready and willing to deliver and requested the buyer to take delivery. Goods not available at the agreed delivery point, coupled with no specific request to take them, fail both requirements.

Conclusion: The seller may have been entitled to suspend or terminate future performance because of the buyer's repudiatory refusal to pay, but cannot recover Section 37 storage or non-acceptance losses for a shipment the seller neither had ready at the agreed place nor offered by a proper request. The distinct contractual consequences should not be conflated.
